changes.before: The women's march and armed Parisian intervention forced unambiguous royal assent to revolutionary decrees and removed the royal family and National Assembly from Versailles to Paris.
changes.after: The women's march and armed Parisian intervention forced unambiguous royal assent to revolutionary decrees and removed the royal family and National Assembly from Versailles to Paris. Deputies wanted freely given royal assent to legitimate their reforms, yet this allowed refusal; popular coercion resolved that dilemma. The king’s transfer preceded the Assembly’s own decision to follow. Delayed royal assent gave way to concessions under October pressure and confinement in Paris. The Assembly sought the king's unambiguous sanction to legitimize the destruction of the old order, while his delays helped provoke direct popular intervention. A mass march from Paris to Versailles secured royal assent to revolutionary measures, exposed the palace to violence, and compelled the monarchy's relocation to Paris. Market women and other female demonstrators initiated and sustained the march that brought the food crisis and royal resistance before the Assembly and king. The October Days relocated the royal family and then the National Assembly from Versailles to Paris, subjecting central institutions to recurring metropolitan pressure. Repeated fears of military or court reversal shaped mobilization until the October Days ended open royal resistance and made revolutionary reform appear irreversible. Reports of banquet insults and fears surrounding the Flanders Regiment were political triggers alongside bread scarcity.

changes.before: The Assembly swept away historically varied provinces and intendancies, creating a uniform decentralized structure of eighty-three departments, districts, and elected communes.
changes.after: The Assembly replaced historically varied provinces and intendancies with eighty-three departments, districts and elected communes, despite mandates defending particular privileges. This uniform but decentralized elected structure also displaced the improvised authorities of July 1789 in 1790. Fear of anarchy and new opportunities for office drew lawyers, businesspeople, merchants, tradesmen, artisans, and other property holders into political administration. Historic liberties and exemptions of provinces, towns, corporations, and judicial bodies were renounced, clearing the way for uniform national institutions. The Assembly replaced France's diverse provinces and jurisdictions with eighty-three departments subdivided into districts and communes governed by elected bodies. The new state combined uniform territorial structures with near-total dependence on locally elected, often unpaid and inexperienced officials. The 1790 local elections replaced the varied committees and arrangements of July 1789 with standardized mayors, procurators, councils, and urban sections. The eligible caption identifies departments of revolutionary France; it adds no geographical access requirement. Weak local enforcement limited administration more broadly than tax collection alone.

changes.before: After the August settlement peasants continued to refuse dues, invade seigneurial property, burn title deeds, plant liberty trees, and pressure lords to surrender rights.
changes.after: Beginning before the August settlement and continuing through 1789–1791, villagers refused dues, attacked seigneurial property, destroyed title deeds and symbols, and compelled renunciations. Later liberty-tree planting asserted that rights had been extinguished. Rural communities transformed political crisis and subsistence anxiety into collective resistance against dues, tithes, taxes, and seigneurial power. Peasants resisted dues and lordly authority by withholding payment, occupying resources, planting liberty trees, and attacking estates or records. Peasant attacks focused on the documentary and material infrastructure that made seigneurial claims enforceable and visible. Rural crowds generally directed violence toward seigneurial claims and escalated destruction when lords resisted, rather than looting indiscriminately. Peasants adapted May-tree customs into political rituals claiming that planted liberty trees could extinguish seigneurial rights.

after.stance: Material and documentary targets made this a practical challenge to dues and authority. Plunder was often limited and violence escalated when lords resisted; legislators nevertheless treated these differentiated practices as attacks on property and order. The author treats peasant action as a decisive independent force that outpaced legislation and continued after the Great Fear subsided. The actions are portrayed as targeted efforts to nullify seigneurial claims, even when illegal and sometimes violent, rather than undirected plunder. The author treats this targeting as evidence of strategic anti-feudal purpose despite the wider fear such destruction generated. The author insists on this distinction while also explaining why legislators and property owners classified all such conduct as lawlessness. The author presents the practice as inventive popular legal symbolism tied to organized pressure on lords.

changes.before: The Revolution replaced venal and privileged officeholding with elected administrators, judges, magistrates, and clergy, while abolishing the parlements and reorganizing courts.
changes.after: The Revolution abolished venal and privileged justice, the parlements and their jurisdictions, replacing them with elected judges and free justice. A hierarchy of justices of the peace, district and criminal courts and a court of cassation accompanied separation of judicial and administrative functions. Courts and local elected authorities lacked reliable enforcement machinery; reliance on municipal administrators and Guards weakened judicial execution. The Revolution abolished sale-based officeholding as incompatible with equality and reconstructed justice, while recognizing many offices as compensable property. Separation of judicial and administrative authority protected against revived despotism but weakened coordination and enforcement. Most public authorities, from administrators and judges to parish priests, were to derive legitimacy through election rather than appointment, purchase, or inherited status. The Assembly eliminated the sovereign courts and old judicial hierarchy as venal, aristocratic, politically obstructive, and incompatible with separated powers. A new hierarchy of justices of the peace, district civil courts, departmental criminal courts, and a national cassation tribunal replaced old-regime courts and introduced juries. Courts were denied administrative authority, while local elected administrators and the National Guard assumed responsibility for order without a dedicated police structure. The Assembly's recognition of abolished offices and some rights as compensable property enlarged public debt and drove later assignat issues.

after.stance: Election also transformed public office more broadly, but judicial reconstruction is distinct from executive–legislative rules. Codification remained unfinished. Compensation for abolished offices created a fiscal obligation without negating the institutional abolition of venality. The author connects venality's destruction to both institutional reform and the mounting fiscal burden of compensation. The reform extends national sovereignty downward but still operates through the restricted active-citizen body. The reform is presented as a complete institutional rupture driven by both principle and patriotic distrust. The architecture rationalizes and separates justice but leaves recodification unfinished and enforcement weak. The arrangement is treated as a vulnerable consequence of the separation of powers and distrust of centralized coercion. Compensation shows the property-minded limits of abolition even as it burdens the revolutionary state financially.

changes.before: The National Assembly's extraordinary all-night session expanded from proposals to calm the countryside into sweeping abolition of feudal, clerical, corporate, provincial, and officeholding privileges.
changes.after: The National Assembly's extraordinary all-night session expanded from proposals to calm the countryside into sweeping abolition of feudal, clerical, corporate, provincial, and officeholding privileges. Provincial and corporate privilege was renounced despite contrary mandates. The subsequent 11 August legal settlement distinguished outright abolition from redeemable dues, while peasant nonpayment made formal compensation largely ineffective. A planned anti-feudal intervention became an emotional all-night session that renounced privileges, dues, offices, ecclesiastical revenues, and corporate exemptions far beyond its original purpose. Breton deputies organized a deliberate dramatic initiative to abolish feudalism and pacify the countryside. Competing noble initiatives for redeeming dues and abolishing serfdom and labour services triggered the escalating renunciations of 4 August. The destruction of legal, fiscal, corporate, provincial, and officeholding privilege became the central social principle of the August settlement. Historic liberties and exemptions of provinces, towns, corporations, and judicial bodies were renounced, clearing the way for uniform national institutions.

after.stance: Fiscal equality and proportional assessment did not ensure collection. Legislators assumed freely consenting citizens would pay, dismantling coercive machinery without an effective compulsory replacement; evasion and obstruction exposed that paradox. changes.before: The electoral system limited voting to tax-qualified adult men, used indirect election, and imposed a high property threshold on deputies despite the Declaration's civil equality.
changes.after: Tax qualifications restricted active citizenship to adult men, with indirect election and successively higher qualifications for electors and deputies. Women were assumed excluded, and many popular participants who had enabled July and October gains were denied formal political power. Declared civil equality contrasted with property-based political eligibility; tax qualification did not make rights universal. Political participation was restricted to tax-paying adult men classified as active citizens, despite the Declaration's language of civil equality. Active citizens chose a much smaller body of wealthier electors, while legislative candidates faced an even higher land and tax threshold. The new citizenship regime excluded women almost without debate and denied political rights to men below the active-citizen tax threshold. Popular mobilization repeatedly enabled the Assembly's victories and secured reform, yet deputies sought to restrict political participation and equip authorities to control crowds.

after.stance: Civil equality did not imply equal political participation. Preserve the active-citizen, elector and deputy hierarchy and the tension between enabling popular action and institutional containment; equal tax assessment alone is not evidence of voting rights. The author emphasizes that the franchise deliberately excluded the popular forces that had rescued the Revolution and was more restrictive than the Estates-General elections. The layered franchise is described as effectively oligarchic and as provoking justified controversy over the silver mark. The exclusions underscore the contradiction between universal civil-rights language and a socially restrictive constitutional electorate. The chapter presents this tension as constitutive of the new order: popular force was indispensable, feared, and progressively bounded by property-based citizenship and coercive law.

changes.after: The 11 August decree declared the feudal regime destroyed but made most dues redeemable; widespread peasant nonpayment made formal compensation largely irrelevant. changes.before: The monarchiens advocated British-style checks, a life senate, and a strong royal veto; the Assembly rejected a second chamber but granted Louis XVI a temporary suspensive veto.
changes.after: The monarchiens advocated British-style checks, a life senate, and a strong royal veto; the Assembly rejected a second chamber but granted Louis XVI a temporary suspensive veto. The Assembly sought the king's unambiguous sanction to legitimize the destruction of the old order, while his delays helped provoke direct popular intervention. Constitutional moderates advocated royal veto power, a life senate, and British-style executive-legislative links to balance the elected Assembly. The Assembly decisively rejected a life senate or second chamber because it appeared to recreate aristocratic privilege and divide the recently unified legislature. The Assembly rejected both an unlimited royal veto and complete absence of veto, choosing a temporary suspensive power as a constitutional compromise. Parisian and provincial activists understood any royal veto as a threat to national sovereignty and used demonstrations, pamphlets, and press agitation against it.

after.stance: Unicameralism and a suspensive royal veto settle central questions of legislative authority; opposition to an absolute veto reflects fear of reversing the Revolution, while the outcome contributes to a weak executive. Deputies sought free royal assent despite its implication that assent might be withheld; Necker hinted that constitutional compromise could secure sanction. Popular hostility to vetoes exceeded the Assembly’s no-veto minority, while the majority accepted a suspensive veto. Distrust of a privileged second chamber was a specific objection. The constitutional problem is presented as a genuine dilemma over free assent and veto, resolved politically by coercive circumstances. The author explains their defeat through distrust of elite privilege, unpopular alliances, and the recent struggle for a unified legislature. The vote is interpreted through political distrust and revolutionary experience rather than abstract constitutional theory alone. The compromise is portrayed as broadly supported within the Assembly but contrary to substantial popular sentiment and linked to expectations of royal assent. The Assembly's adoption of a suspensive veto is identified as its first clear defiance of popular sentiment.

changes.after: Refusing bankruptcy, the Assembly postponed the debt problem as failed loans and an underperforming Patriotic Contribution exposed the inadequacy of Necker’s finance. The one-time quarter-income levy relied on unverified declarations. Inherited debt and compensation obligations continued to drive the search for Church-land and paper finance. Inherited debt, collapsing revenue, failed loans, compensation obligations, and growing deficits forced the Assembly toward Church-land nationalization and assignat finance. A one-time levy of one quarter of citizen income was adopted as an emergency fiscal measure but lacked verification and yielded far below its target. The unresolved debt burden drove paper assignat finance as well as the prior Church-land proposal. The Extraordinary Fund was to receive proceeds of the Patriotic Contribution and national-land sales.

before.label: Necker’s declining financial authority and resignation
before.meaning: Revenue miscalculation, opposition to expanding assignats, radical hostility, and loss of legislative influence destroyed Necker's credibility and led to his resignation in September 1790.
before.stance: The former national hero and his financial methods are portrayed as superseded by the revolutionary order he helped bring about.

after.label: Necker’s declining financial authority and resignation
after.meaning: Revenue miscalculation, opposition to expanding assignats, radical hostility, and loss of legislative influence destroyed Necker's credibility and led to his resignation in September 1790. His proposed bank alternative failed amid memories of Law, suspicion of financiers and competing financial interests. Necker's public authority eroded through failed loans, political equivocation, an inadequate emergency levy, mistaken deficit projections, and resistance to Church confiscation and paper finance.
after.stance: The former national hero and his financial methods are portrayed as superseded by the revolutionary order he helped bring about. Distinguish those objections from opposition to expanding assignats; the source establishes loss of authority and resignation, not a measured absence of public response. The author presents his fall as the eclipse of both a once-popular minister and the old financial methods he represented.

after.evidence_summary: Talleyrand and Mirabeau advanced distinct proposals and ownership arguments; opponents invoked protected property and supporters and opponents disputed the effects of land sales on the market.
Hostile gallery pressure accompanied nationalization; most deputies already expected fundamental Church reform and treated clerical resistance as self-interested special pleading.

changes.before: Facing debt and the loss of tithes, the Assembly placed all clerical property at the nation's disposal after a debate over ownership, rights, clergy support, and land-sale consequences.
changes.after: Debt and lost tithes prompted competing plans for Church property. Talleyrand’s proposal and Mirabeau’s ownership argument challenged clerical corporate property while opponents invoked the Declaration and religious endowments; supporters anticipated wider landownership, opponents a depressed land market. Hostile gallery pressure accompanied the Assembly’s placing property at the nation’s disposal and assuming clerical maintenance. To meet the financial emergency, the Assembly placed ecclesiastical property at the nation's disposal while assuming responsibility for clerical maintenance and Church functions. Debate over Church lands opposed corporate and institutional ownership claims to theories that the clergy merely administered property for the nation and no longer existed as an order. Talleyrand gave episcopal authority to a partial fiscal use of Church property, while Mirabeau moved the broader formula that allowed national disposal of the whole. Many deputies and gallery spectators interpreted clerical objections as corporate self-interest, making Church property and institutional autonomy politically vulnerable.

after.stance: Keep ownership, market and maintenance arguments distinct. Deputies’ expectations of fundamental Church reform encouraged them to view clerical resistance as self-interested. Retain the source’s November 3 vote dating without silently correcting it from outside sources. The decision is explained by fiscal necessity, pre-existing reform hostility, and theories of corporate trusteeship, while the property-rights objection is treated as substantive. changes.before: The Assembly broadly fulfilled demands for constitutional monarchy, representation, equality, and liberty but enacted many transformative measures absent or ambiguous in the cahiers; these changes nevertheless won wide initial support.
changes.after: The Assembly broadly fulfilled demands for constitutional monarchy, representation, equality, and liberty but enacted many transformative measures absent or ambiguous in the cahiers; these changes nevertheless won wide initial support. This consensus coexisted with disorderly implementation and injured interests; nobles, clergy, officeholders and wider society actively contributed to reconstruction. Many decisive reforms lacked electoral mandates and arose as contingent responses to unprecedented events rather than execution of a pre-existing national program. Despite chaotic execution and injured interests, reform attracted meaningful participation from nobles, clerics, officeholders, peasants, and bourgeois citizens. Most of the first year's far-reaching changes won substantial acceptance across French society before that consensus began to disintegrate.

after.stance: The source concludes that revolutionary process and unprecedented events, not a settled national program, generated much of the reform; acceptance was broad but already disintegrating by July 1791. Widespread first-year support does not make every measure mandated by the cahiers or its implementation orderly. This is the chapter's central interpretive conclusion: the first year's transformation was produced by revolution itself, even where broad constitutional aims matched the cahiers. The author identifies a real, not merely ceremonial, national consensus while making its exclusions, strains, and short duration explicit.

changes.before: The removal of clerical revenues, feudal rights, property, and institutional autonomy from 1789 through the dissolution of most monasteries and convents in 1790.
changes.after: Initially cooperative clergy confronted cumulative loss of revenues, feudal rights, property and autonomy. Utility-based suppression closed most monasteries and convents while retaining functional exceptions and prohibiting new binding vows. State dependence raised minimum salaries for some priests but brought cuts or uncertain payment for others; inventories and sales turned reform into local loyalty tests. Clerical deputies initially helped transform the Estates-General while expecting reform, not destruction of the clergy’s corporate status or autonomy. The abolition of tithes, dues, pluralism, and papal payments, followed by nationalization of Church property, removed the clergy’s independent material base and made it dependent on state salaries. The Assembly dissolved most regular religious houses and prohibited new vows, retaining only institutions serving education or charity. The nation seized ecclesiastical estates, inventoried them, and prepared their sale while taking responsibility for charitable and educational functions. After taking ecclesiastical property, the nation promised salaries to clergy and assumed responsibility for education and charity, making the Church materially dependent on the state.

after.meaning: Initially cooperative clergy confronted cumulative loss of revenues, feudal rights, property and autonomy. Utility-based suppression closed most monasteries and convents while retaining functional exceptions and prohibiting new binding vows. State dependence raised minimum salaries for some priests but brought cuts or uncertain payment for others; inventories and sales turned reform into local loyalty tests. Clerical deputies initially helped transform the Estates-General while expecting reform, not destruction of the clergy’s corporate status or autonomy. The abolition of tithes, dues, pluralism, and papal payments, followed by nationalization of Church property, removed the clergy’s independent material base and made it dependent on state salaries. The Assembly dissolved most regular religious houses and prohibited new vows, retaining only institutions serving education or charity. The nation seized ecclesiastical estates, inventoried them, and prepared their sale while taking responsibility for charitable and educational functions. after.stance: Individual precedents did not remove alarm at the cumulative destruction of corporate independence. Early goodwill was not consent to that outcome, and material effects differed across the clergy. The author rejects hindsight: early clerical cooperation did not constitute consent to the far-reaching ecclesiastical settlement that followed. The author presents these measures as a sequence of losses that turned much clerical enthusiasm into a sense of dispossession despite promised income and public functions. The author explains the policy through Enlightenment utility and recent reform precedent while stressing that Catholics perceived it as another element of a hostile pattern. The author treats confiscation as both a fiscal and constitutional transformation whose local enforcement helped polarize religion. The author notes that salary reform benefited poorly paid priests but reduced other incomes and created uncertainty over when payment would begin.

He led patriotic efforts to pressure clerical deputies toward the oath.
Le Chapelier and the triumvirate concluded that the Revolution had to stop and the constitution be consolidated.
Former radicals concluded that further Revolution threatened existing gains and that the constitution needed completion and implementation.
Barnave, Duport, and the Lameths moderated out of concern for the monarchy’s constitutional role and their own future political influence.
By early summer he and the triumvirate were moderating to preserve monarchy and future influence.
The triumvirate's move toward the center aroused popular suspicion and helped elevate Robespierre's group.
Their move to the center elevated a smaller left opposition around Robespierre.
He defended slavery and warned against free-colored political claims before Robespierre defeated his position.
Monarchist Jacobins seceded to create the Feuillant Club after the republican petition crisis.
Most active Jacobins and nearly all deputies seceded to the Feuillants, leaving Robespierre, Pétion, and a few allies behind.

Right-wing elites withheld support, most provincial clubs remained Jacobin, and no major Paris paper adopted the Feuillant cause.
Only a small minority of provincial affiliates permanently followed the Feuillants, limiting their national organizational success.
Foreign-war rumors and émigré intrigue preserved polarization despite attempts at conciliation.

changes.before: The movement of former radicals toward consolidation of the Revolution, preservation of monarchy, and the creation of the Feuillant political organization.
changes.after: Barnave, Duport and the Lameths moved from radical reform to consolidation, fearing loss of both monarchy as the constitutional keystone and their future influence. After the petition crisis they seceded from the Jacobins as Feuillants; the remaining Jacobins withdrew from the petition. Barnave’s accommodation included a conservative colonial exception. Le Chapelier, Barnave, Duport, and the Lameths moved from radical leadership toward consolidation, preservation of monarchy, and control of popular pressure. changes.before: The Assembly's comprehensive reorganization of the French Church, including diocesan rationalization, elected clergy, residence rules, salaried ministry, and reduced papal authority.
changes.after: The Assembly's comprehensive reorganization of the French Church, including diocesan rationalization, elected clergy, residence rules, salaried ministry, and reduced papal authority. Diocesan rationalization followed departmental organization; election extended to clergy, residence and salaries altered careers, and papal spiritual communion was nominally retained while confirmation became notification. Later ordinary-law status meant the general constitutional oath did not itself require acceptance of the Civil Constitution. The July 1790 settlement reconstructed the French Church as a salaried, territorially rationalized, electorally staffed national institution subordinated in temporal organization to the revolutionary state. A lay-dominated Assembly committee pursued a leaner Church modeled rhetorically on early-Christian discipline and denied the Pope authority over France’s temporal religious organization. The Assembly wound up the Concordat without replacement and rejected episcopal requests for a national council to consent to reform. The Civil Constitution reduced dioceses and parishes, abolished nonpastoral benefices, imposed residence and service requirements, and established public salary scales. Bishops and parish priests were to be elected through secular citizen assemblies, while episcopal advisory councils echoed Richerist calls for less hierarchical Church government. The Civil Constitution prohibited ordinary ties to foreign bishops and reduced papal confirmation of French bishops to notification, while French clerics sought a papal response that might preserve communion. Bishops who opposed the Civil Constitution defended ecclesiastical consultation, while local authorities enforced the law through expulsions, dissolutions, elections, dismissal, and salary suspension. The committee that designed comprehensive Church reform acquired a stronger lay majority when clerical members resisted the breadth of proposed change. Richerist traditions favored election and priestly synods as checks on episcopal hierarchy, influencing advisory councils in the Civil Constitution.

after.stance: Distinguish administrative reconstruction from doctrinal claims, nominal communion from reduced jurisdiction, and the specific clerical oath from the constitutional oath. These institutional distinctions mattered to contested legitimacy and resistance. The author sees many administrative reforms as defensible and acceptable, but identifies unilateral state action, lay election, and papal displacement as the provisions that made schism likely. The author notes that only a minority were freethinking anti-clericals; most reformers understood themselves as sincere Catholics, which makes the ensuing conflict more than a simple secular assault. The author treats rejection of ecclesiastical consultation as a crucial procedural error: it left no French Church authority capable of offsetting a papal condemnation. The author distinguishes these practical reforms from the appointment and papal questions, judging much of the rationalization reasonable and potentially acceptable to most clergy. The author stresses that clerical reform traditions did not entail election by lay bodies that might include non-Catholics or unbelievers. The author treats schism as foreseeable but not initially desired by most French clergy or even by the temporizing Pope. The author distinguishes the bishops’ restrained constitutional argument from the insurrectionary meaning attributed to it by patriots. The author distinguishes a small freethinking minority from the larger group of sincere Catholic reformers, preventing the committee from being reduced to simple anti-religious intent. The author limits the analogy: Richerists did not advocate unrestricted lay election by religiously mixed citizen bodies.

Religious estrangement was important but his flight manifesto also attacked the constitutional, property and public-order settlement. after.stance: Although Louis sanctioned revolutionary measures, his personal religious commitments and experience of coercion drove him toward escape and made his later constitutional acceptance appear insincere. Intentions beyond Montmédy remain uncertain. The earlier Saint-Cloud excursion is not proved to have been an escape attempt; court planning and the queen’s role require their own qualified treatment. The author assigns the religious schism a direct role in the king’s alienation while distinguishing the queen’s earlier rescue hopes from the king’s later independent decision. The author treats the manifesto as clear evidence that the king had renounced the Revolution, regardless of uncertainty over his intended destination after Montmédy.

Intentions beyond Montmédy remain uncertain. The earlier Saint-Cloud excursion is not proved to have been an escape attempt; court planning and the queen’s role require their own qualified treatment. The author assigns the religious schism a direct role in the king’s alienation while distinguishing the queen’s earlier rescue hopes from the king’s later independent decision. The author treats the manifesto as clear evidence that the king had renounced the Revolution, regardless of uncertainty over his intended destination after Montmédy.

changes.before: The growth of the Paris Jacobin society and its provincial affiliates as institutions for political debate, mobilization, communication, and enforcement of revolutionary policy.
changes.after: Drawing on earlier associational practices, Paris Jacobins and provincial affiliates expanded through local political issues, debate, correspondence, petitions and enforcement of revolutionary policy. Varennes caused a surge in membership and demands for deposition or trial, but few explicitly endorsed a republic and the Paris mother society left the monarchy question unresolved, admitting outside radical pressure. The petition crisis produced Feuillant secession, Jacobin withdrawal from that petition and continued Jacobin allegiance among most affiliates. Southern clubs were galvanized by the Jalès movement, while religious newspapers and the clerical oath made religious conflict an immediate organizing issue. The Paris Society of the Friends of the Constitution and its provincial affiliates formed a rapidly expanding national political network that debated policy, sustained enthusiasm, pressured authorities, and circulated patriotic information. The royal flight produced nationwide expectations of Austrian intervention, Guard mobilization, vigilance committees, attacks on refractories, and intense political-club participation. Committed constitutional monarchists, including Lafayette and the triumvirate, left the Jacobins after the anti-restoration petition and founded a rival Society of the Friends of the Constitution at the Feuillants.

changes.before: The compulsory oath imposed on beneficed clergy, the division between constitutional priests and nonjurors, and the regional and social pattern of acceptance and refusal.
changes.after: The compulsory oath imposed on beneficed clergy, the division between constitutional priests and nonjurors, and the regional and social pattern of acceptance and refusal. The oath became a kind of opinion poll on the Revolution: local origins and parish solidarity helped western priests refuse, alongside economic incentives and official pressure elsewhere. Contrasting regional patterns and the final national synthesis remain part of the requirement. Beneficed clergy were required publicly to swear fidelity to nation, king, law, and the Assembly’s constitution, with refusal bringing replacement under the Civil Constitution. Oath-taking varied sharply by region according to clerical economy, cultural distance, earlier anti-episcopal activism, local political pressure, and ties between parish priests and communities. A priest’s oath or refusal frequently expressed parish opinion on the Revolution far beyond ecclesiastical organization; the overall result indicated a large constituency that believed change had gone far enough. Nonjurors rejected the oath and often retained strong parish support, becoming a large, geographically concentrated body whose worship and political loyalty were contested. The oath defined rival constitutional and refractory camps.

after.meaning: The compulsory oath imposed on beneficed clergy, the division between constitutional priests and nonjurors, and the regional and social pattern of acceptance and refusal. after.stance: The oath is judged the Constituent Assembly’s gravest error because it compelled public choice and legitimized organized dissent. Distinguish roughly half initially refusing, about 54 percent of parish clergy ultimately swearing, and later retractions among constitutionals; local solidarity and pressure matter alongside income. Distinguish complying episcopal deputies in the Assembly from the later national episcopal count. Regional examples derive from prose, and collective solidarity should not be reduced to individual career calculation. The author calls the oath one of the Revolution’s great turning points and the Constituent Assembly’s gravest error because it compelled public choice, legitimized dissent, and divided roughly half the clergy. The author rejects a single material explanation and gives exceptional importance to lay pressure and local solidarity. The author treats the oath as a proxy for wider political consent, not merely a test of clerical doctrine or income. The author rejects the Assembly’s expectation of a tiny episcopal faction and shows refractories as central to popular opposition and counter-revolution.

changes.before: The practical staffing of the reorganized Church and the new career opportunities opened to lower clergy, former monks, and canons by election and episcopal refusal.
changes.after: The practical staffing of the reorganized Church and the new career opportunities opened to lower clergy, former monks, and canons by election and episcopal refusal. Legitimacy remained contested, and papal intervention prompted withdrawals and retractions. The oath opened episcopal and parish careers to sworn clergy, former regulars, and previously excluded talent, while widespread refusal produced vacancies, shortages, and temporary reliance on nonjurors. Clergy who swore the oath staffed the reorganized national Church, gained new avenues of promotion, and faced contested legitimacy after papal intervention. Staff shortages forced temporary use of refractory priests despite the rival camps defined by the oath.

changes.before: Popular political societies that organized republican petitioning and mass mobilization after Varennes.
changes.after: Earlier Cordeliers organization and the Social Circle’s utopian discussion developed into popular petitioning and mass mobilization after Varennes. They demanded deposition or popular determination of the monarchy question and continued the Champ de Mars petition after Jacobin withdrawal. Popular societies, newspapers and neighborhood activists sustained mobilization that Lafayette attempted to contain. Varennes brought republicanism into open politics as the Cordeliers and Social Circle demanded deposition or national consultation and drafted a petition treating the crown as vacant. The Society of the Friends of the Rights of Man fostered popular societies, supported anti-royal mobilization, demanded deposition or national consultation after Varennes, and continued the republican petition after the Jacobins withdrew. A Paris club known before Varennes for utopian discussion became an organizer and publisher of republican opposition through the Bouche de fer and mass intervention at the Jacobins. Repression after Champ de Mars suppressed clubs and popular organizers; petition organizers did not implement the massacre.

changes.after: Robespierre rose as former radicals moderated, denounced slavery and defended political rights regardless of colour. changes.before: The conflict after Varennes between republican demands for deposition or popular decision and the Assembly majority's determination to preserve constitutional monarchy.
changes.after: The Assembly governed effectively during Louis XVI’s suspension yet preserved monarchy through a conscious kidnapping fiction, fearing a regency, reopened constitutional debate and empowerment of popular forces. The post-Varennes dispute divided proponents of deposition, trial or popular consultation from defenders of the settlement. The Constituent Assembly governed without the king, suspended his functions, blamed Bouillé and advisers, and publicly pretended that the monarch had been abducted so the nearly completed monarchy-centered constitution could survive.

changes.before: The post-Varennes acceleration of aristocratic and military emigration, the Assembly's penalties, and the loss of much of the army's officer corps.
changes.after: The post-Varennes acceleration of aristocratic and military emigration, the Assembly's penalties, and the loss of much of the army's officer corps. The August 1 return deadline, official lists and triple taxation were followed by September repeal and amnesty; neither penalties nor conciliation arrested departure. The Assembly imposed return deadlines, taxation, and official lists on émigrés, while Varennes and a reordered military oath accelerated the departure of nobles and thousands of officers and deepened mutiny. The Assembly ordered émigrés home, imposed triple taxation, and created official lists, before later repealing the law in an amnesty. A reordered loyalty oath and the Varennes débâcle accelerated the departure of roughly six thousand officers, more than half the corps.
